claims.text: Conventional EAM references poorly represent the many atomic configurations present in ab initio liquids of multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
An actively learned neural-network potential or Gaussian Approximation Potential can be trained on ab initio configurations spanning crystalline and liquid states.
Active learning can tailor an MLIP training set to a specified class of alloy systems and properties.
Enriching the training set with diverse liquid-state and near-melting ab initio configurations will adequately cover the relevant configuration space.
MLIPs use descriptors representing local chemical and structural atomic environments.
Atom-centered symmetry functions or smooth-overlap-of-atomic-positions descriptors encode the relevant local environments in the proposed MLIP.
Compositionally complex alloys exhibit local chemical fluctuations and a large combinatorial configuration space.
Simple EAM potentials represent complex local chemical fluctuations and many-body interactions less accurately than the proposed MLIP.
Training on a broad ab initio configuration space will improve phase-space overlap between the MLIP reference and the ab initio target.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The MLIP reference will markedly reduce TI path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The reduction in TI path mismatch may be a factor of 2–3.
The proposed method applies to refractory or compositionally complex high-entropy alloys, including systems such as Nb–Mo–Ta, in both solid and liquid states near melting.
The method may offer less benefit for alloys with simpler chemistry or at much lower temperatures where the liquid phase is not sampled.
MLIP performance depends on the quality and diversity of training data across the relevant phase space.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing otherwise parallel EAM-reference and MLIP-reference TI calculations against fully converged ab initio free-energy calculations.
Structural order parameters and liquid diffusion coefficients can be used to verify accurate capture of many-body interactions.
The hypothesis is falsified if the MLIP yields less than a 1.2-fold statistically significant improvement in TI path mismatch or fails to improve phase-space overlap over EAM.
